chunks.document_content: Keywords Diabetic macular edema, Topical NSAIDs, BCVA, CMT ​Introduction Background Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is one of the most common chronic diseases worldwide and poses significant chal­ lenges to patient health. In 2021, the worldwide preva­ lence of diabetes in 20-79 years old adults was reported to be 10.5% (536.6 million people) and is expected to rise to 12.2% (783.2 million people) in 2045 [1]. Objective In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to compare the outcomes of using topical NSAIDs in patients with DME, both as stand-alone therapy and as an adjunct to other treatment modalities. Methods This systematic review was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) [10]. Studies pertaining to the treatment diabetic macular edema using NSAIDS ver­ sus anti-VEGF were reviewed and screened, with those matching the pre-determined eligibility criteria selected and further analyzed. In patients with uncontrolled diabetes, persistent hyperglycemia causes long-term vascular damage to sev­ eral organs, resulting in macrovascular and microvascu­ lar complications. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication in patients with diabetes, with an estimated global prevalence of 191 mil­ lion patients by 2030 [2]. The primary outcome of this study was improvement in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Secondary out­ comes included central macular thickness (CMT), macu­ lar volume, and treatment complications. DR is classified into two stages: non-proliferative dia­ betic retinopathy (NPDR) and proliferative diabetic reti­ nopathy (PDR). NPDR is the early stage of DR, in which key features include the formation of microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs). PDR is characterized by neovas­ cularization, which can lead to various vision-threatening complications. In addition, patients may develop diabetic macular edema (DME) at any stage of DR [3]. Eligibility criteria All clinical trials that compared the use of NSAIDs with other agents in patients with DME were included. Indi­ viduals of all ages, sexes, races, ethnicities, and comor­ bidity statuses were included. The exclusion criteria included studies that were not performed in humans, studies that were predominantly focused on other dia­ betic ocular pathologies, studies that mainly focused on the use of NSAIDs after cataract surgery, the use of intravitreal NSAIDs, and studies that were conducted on a cohort not representative of the general patient popu­ lation. After conducting a literature search, 68 published studies were reviewed using this eligibility criteria, with 62 studies excluded, yielding only 6 studies qualifying for inclusion in this review. DME is a common complication of diabetes and one of the leading causes of significant vision loss globally. Chronic hyperglycemia and retinal hypoxia stimulate the production of VEGF, resulting in vascular hyperper­ meability with intra- and subretinal thickening, which results in the development of DME [4, 5]. Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are considered the first-line treatment in the management of DME [5]. Some disadvantages of the use of such agents include the need for re-injection, short-term effects, and the risk of complications. Search strategy and selection of studies The literature search was conducted using several medi­ cal databases, to search for relevant articles published on the topic.

When a meta-analysis was not deemed suitable for an outcome, it was pooled qualita­ tively and presented either in text or tabular format, highlighting the characteristics of each included study. Meta-analysis: primary and secondary outcomes BCVA The primary outcome of this study was the improve­ ment in best-corrected visual acuity using ETDRS let­ ters as the units. All data displayed in other units such as logMAR, was converted to ETDRS letters. A meta-analysis was performed with three studies and the results are displayed in a forest plot (Fig. 3). This meta-analysis was done using a fixed-effects model. The sample size for this meta-analysis was 245 patients, with 121 patients receiving topical NSAIDs either solely or in addition to the intervention and 124 patients receiving the control. The findings showed a statistically significant difference (P = 0.04) in the mean difference between the two groups, with the results favoring the NSAIDs group. The pooled mean difference was 1.82 with a 95% CI 0.12-3.53. There was moderate heterogeneity (I2:60%, p = 0.08) observed among the studies. Methodological quality and risk of bias assessment The quality and risk of bias of all included articles was assessed using Cochrane's collaborative tool for random­ ized controlled trials and the Newcastle Ottawa scale for non-randomized studies. The Cochrane Collaboration tool assesses several domains, including selection, perfor­ mance, attrition, and reporting biases [11]. The Newcas­ tle Ottawa uses a star-based grading system to assess the methodological quality of observational studies, based on selection, quality, and outcome, with a maximum score of nine stars [12]. Results Literature search results The search yielded 68 articles, which were screened by reviewing their titles and abstracts to exclude dupli­ cates and irrelevant articles.
